nameStory: The poet's narcissus gets its romantic name from ancient Greek mythology, where the beautiful youth Narcissus fell in love with his own reflection and was transformed into this flower. It's also called 'pheasant's eye' because the small red-rimmed center of the white flower resembles a bird's bright eye. This elegant spring bloomer has inspired countless poems and stories throughout history.
description: Poet's narcissus is a graceful spring bulb flower that stands about 12-18 inches tall on a single sturdy stem. Each stem produces one pristine white flower with six pointed petals surrounding a small, flat yellow center ringed with bright red or orange. The narrow, blue-green leaves emerge directly from the ground in small clumps, creating an elegant garden display. Unlike many daffodils, this species has a distinctly sweet, almost intoxicating fragrance.

idTips.label: Flowers

habitat: Found in old gardens, abandoned homesites, and naturalized areas throughout New England where it has escaped cultivation. Prefers well-drained soils in partial shade to full sun, often persisting for decades in forgotten corners of properties. Commonly seen along old stone walls, near cellar holes, and in overgrown meadows where historical settlements once stood.

seasonality.spring: Blooms in late spring (May-June) after most other daffodils have finished, producing intensely fragrant white flowers. Leaves emerge earlier and are fully developed by bloom time.
seasonality.summer: Leaves remain green into early summer before gradually yellowing and dying back. Seed capsules develop and mature during this period.
seasonality.fall: Completely dormant with no visible parts above ground. New bulb growth begins underground in preparation for next year.
seasonality.winter: Dormant underground as bulbs. No visible parts above ground, but roots may continue growing slowly in unfrozen soil.

funFact: This flower was so prized in ancient times that it may be the original narcissus mentioned in Greek mythology - making it possibly the world's first 'celebrity' flower, famous for over 2,000 years!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with paperwhite narcissus, but poet's narcissus has the telltale red rim around its yellow center (paperwhites have plain white or yellow centers) and blooms much later in the season. Remember: if it has a 'red eye' and blooms in late spring, it's the poet's narcissus.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'narcissus,' this plant belongs to the same family as onions and garlic, which explains why deer and rodents typically avoid eating the bulbs. The bulbs contain toxic compounds that were once used medicinally but can be dangerous if consumed.
compareHints: Unlike the familiar yellow trumpet daffodils (Narcissus pseudonarcissus) that bloom earlier, poet's narcissus has pure white petals and a flat, small center rather than a large trumpet. It also blooms much later than most daffodils and has that distinctive red rim around the corona. Compared to bunch-flowered daffodils, poet's narcissus produces only one flower per stem rather than clusters.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Wild daffodil differs from its Narcissus relatives by having pale yellow petals rather than the pure white of Poet's Narcissus or Paperwhite, and produces single flowers rather than the clusters seen in Bunch-flowered Daffodil.
Unlike wild daffodil which has one large flower per stem, this species always has multiple smaller flowers clustered together.

Unlike other daffodils in New England, the hoop-petticoat has an enormous corona that completely dominates tiny, thread-like petals - the exact opposite of poet's narcissus which has huge white petals and a tiny orange cup.
Unlike other New England daffodils that bloom singly in spring with thick, substantial petals, paperwhite produces clusters of smaller flowers with distinctively thin, translucent petals.
Angel's-tears differs from other New England daffodils by its tiny size, pure white color, and distinctly drooping flowers.
